---
title: 'Image analysis'
title-block-banner: false
---

A course on the mathematics and methods of digital image analysis, for students
who have studied linear algebra and calculus. Most of image analysis turns out to
be linear algebra and calculus in disguise: an image is a matrix, a geometric
transform is a matrix acting on coordinates, a filter is a linear map, and the
Fourier transform is a change of basis.

The course is built around **interactive demos**: change the input, and see what
happens. Every unit has one; the [demo gallery](demos.qmd) lists them all.

## How each unit works

Work through the sidebar from top to bottom. Each unit has:

- a **lecture** (slides, green in the sidebar),
- a **quiz** (blue): short questions to check your understanding,
- an **exercise**: questions to do by hand, then an **interactive demo** (orange) with questions to explore.

Do the pen-and-paper questions first, then use the demo to check and extend them.

The material comes in two layers. The **ideas** (pictures, demos, plain explanations and small examples with numbers) are complete on their own. The **math** (formulas, derivations, proofs) is clearly marked: slides titled *The math* with a "math layer" badge, and questions tagged *(math)*. On a first pass you can skim the math and still follow every idea; come back to it when you want the full story.

## Topics

The course is organised in five parts of one-day topics, plus electives.

- **Part I: Images as numbers**: images, filters, frequencies and principal components; edges, blobs and ridges; bit depth and noise; image formation; deconvolution.
- **Part II: From pixels to objects**: thresholding, colour, morphology, labelling, watershed and measurements.
- **Part III: Aligning images**: registration in frequency space (FFT registration).
- **Part IV: Segmentation as optimisation**: graph cuts (energy minimisation, maximum flow, graph-cut segmentation, normalized cuts).
- **Part V: Learning from examples**: random forests, neural networks, evaluation and statistics, variational autoencoders and modern deep learning.
- **Electives**, each taken after a core day: *Objects* (skeletons, moments), *Curves and energies* (splines and NURBS, snakes and active shape models, level sets, dynamic programming, Ising models and Markov random fields), *Detection* (Hough transform, integral images, point detection), *Motion* (optical flow, tracking), *More learning* (support vector machines, Gaussian mixtures), *Generative models* (diffusion models), *Transforms* (wavelets, image compression, Radon transform and tomography), *Spectral* (spectral unmixing), *Fluorescence quantification* (colocalisation, FRET, fluorescence lifetime imaging), *3D* (marching cubes, 3D graphics, geometry from multiple images, ray tracing) and *Computing* (how GPUs work).
